Lesson 16: Philosophy & Worldview 
The word worldview refers to the sum total of all your beliefs, knowledge, 
understanding, philosophy, and values. Your worldview is shaped and 
influenced by your culture, your religion (or lack thereof), and your 
upbringing – as well as your own ideas and ideals. 
In today’s lesson we’re going to learn some general terms for talking about 
different worldviews and their elements. 
Worldview Basics 
One of the most basic divisions that influences peoples’ worldview is belief or 
disbelief in a higher power.  
• Religions like Christianity and Islam are monotheistic – they believe in 
only ONE god.  
• Religions like Hinduism are polytheistic – they believe in many gods 
and goddesses.  
• Some tribal religions are pantheistic – believing that nature or the 
universe is god, and god is inside everything in creation.  
• The belief that there is no god is called atheism, and someone who 
believes this is an atheist. 
Instead of a god, some people believe in fate or destiny – an impersonal force 
that controls everything in the universe – and that events are predetermined 
or predestined to occur. Others disagree, arguing that humans have free will 
– the ability to choose their actions independently. 
When someone officially adopts a religion, they have converted. Organized 
religions have doctrines or tenets – specific principles held as true. One word 
to describe the entire set of these principles is dogma – but this word 
sometimes has a negative connotation, often used to refer to principles that 
are accepted without thinking, questioning, or doubting. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
There is no perfect religion or philosophy; you’ll often find contradictions or 
paradoxes – apparently impossible situations/beliefs that are still 
supposedly true. And at the root of all belief systems are certain underlying 
assumptions – things that are assumed to be true without evidence or proof.  
Some people think that there are no real philosophical certainties; it’s all 
conjecture – inferences and conclusions from incomplete evidence. 
The belief that moral and ethical “truths” are relative, and depend on the 
situation and people involved, is called relativism. 
The Most Common -ISMs 
A lot of philosophical ideas end in –ism, like atheism and relativism as you 
learned earlier in this lesson. There are hundreds of “isms”, but I’m going to 
teach you the most common ones. 
With each of the “isms,” you’re learning three words in one. Let’s take 
optimism as an example – the tendency to dwell on the positive: 
• optimism (n.) = the philosophy, the belief 
• optimist (n.) = a person who holds that belief 
• optimistic (adj.) = the descriptive adjective 
an optimistic article, an optimistic person, an optimistic view 
You can use these endings, –ist for the person and –istic for the adjective, for 
all the –ism words you’re about to learn. By the way, do you know what the 
opposite of optimism is? It’s pessimism – dwelling on the negative. 
One major dichotomy – a strong division between two contrasting things – is 
between realism and idealism. An idealist envisions things in an ideal or 
perfect manner, and thinks that our beliefs can change reality. A realist is 
more pragmatic (practical, dealing with real facts) and focuses on what 
actually exists in reality, not an imaginary version. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
Humanism is a belief that rejects religion, 
but places a high value on humans and their 
capacities and worth. Anybody, whether 
religious or not, is capable of altruism – that 
means unselfish concern for the well-being 
of others.  
Some cultures and societies place a very 
high value on living together in community 
and depending on each other, whereas 
others emphasize individualism, a focus on the self-reliance and 
independence of each individual. 
Hedonism is the belief that pleasure and the pursuit of pleasure is the 
primary goal – especially sensual pleasures like eating, drinking, and sex.  
Pacifism is the belief that conflicts should always be settled peacefully, 
without violence and war. Feminism is the belief in the equality of men and 
women. 
Belief and Doubt 
Are you gullible? People who are gullible believe everything they read/hear 
without investigating or considering if it is really true. This type of person can 
be easily influenced and easily deceived.  
Or are you skeptical? A skeptical person doubts and questions everything, 
especially established facts. A skeptical person is difficult to persuade or 
convince. 
Another type of person is a fanatic – this is someone who has a strong and 
extreme enthusiasm for a certain belief or cause. Some fanatics have radical 
beliefs – the word “radical” means a very large departure from what is 
traditional or customary.

Lesson 17: Describing the World 
Climate 
Climate is different from weather - the word climate describes the general 
conditions of temperature and precipitation (how much rain/snow overall), 
whereas weather describes the temporary conditions which change every 
day. 
An arid climate is one that is very dry, where there is not enough water for 
much vegetation to grow - typically only cacti or small shrubs. 
 
 
A tropical climate is hot and humid (meaning there's a lot of moisture in the 
air). Some regions with tropical climates are prone to monsoons - seasons of 
very heavy rain. 
 
A temperate climate has moderate temperatures, which often vary by season, 
and mild weather, and an arctic/polar climate is extremely cold. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
 
Vegetation 
The vegetation varies based on the climate. Tropical climates have jungles or 
rain forests, with large trees and great biodiversity. The tops of the trees 
form a canopy, a thick layer that blocks most sunlight. 
 
In more temperate climates, we call an area of dense trees a forest or woods. 
Two types of trees are evergreen trees - trees that keep their leaves during 
all four seasons - and deciduous trees, which completely lose their foliage 
(leaves) during the winter or dry season, then grow it back in the springtime. 
 
 
Evergreen and deciduous trees 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
A savanna is a more open area, where the trees are scattered. A scrubland 
has mostly bushes and grasses rather than trees, and a prairie has virtually 
no trees, mostly grasses. 
 
 
savanna, scrubland, and prairie 
As you might imagine from the name, a wetland is an area where the ground 
is saturated with water. Finally, there is tundra – an area where very little 
vegetation grows due to cold climate or high altitude. 
 
 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
wetland and tundra 
Geographical Features 
You already know the basics like mountains, rivers, and valleys – so let’s go a 
little further into specific geographical features. 
A group or chain of islands is called an archipelago. The country of Greece 
has an archipelago. When there’s a part of land that’s surrounded on three 
sides by water but still connected to the mainland, that’s a peninsula. This is 
the Arabian peninsula in the Middle East. 
 
Greek archipelago and Arabian peninsula 
The opposite – a section of the ocean that is partly surrounded by land, so that 
the waters become calmer – is called a bay. A large bay is called a gulf – like 
the Gulf of Mexico. 
 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
In deserts and near beaches, we have sand dunes – hills or mountains of sand 
that can shift with the wind. In the middle of a desert, there can be an isolated 
area of vegetation called an oasis. These often form around springs – sources 
of water coming up from the ground. 
 
 
sand dunes and oasis 
Let’s look at some more mountainous vocabulary. A plateau is a raised area 
with a flat top. It can be small or very large, covering an entire region. When 
you have a rock face that is vertical or near vertical, this is a cliff. Finally, areas 
of flat or gently rolling terrain are called plains. 
 
 
 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
plateau, cliff, and plains 
Using the Land 
Two major ways to use the land are agriculture and mining. 
Plants that are grown for food – rice, corn, fruit, vegetables, etc. are called 
crops. Farmers plant seeds and then harvest (collect) the crops when they 
are ready. 
 
harvesting crops 
It may be necessary to fertilize the soil – add natural or artificial substances 
to provide more nutrients and help the crops grow better. In areas where 
there is little rainfall, irrigation is needed to artificially apply water to the 
soil. To eliminate insects which can eat and damage the crops, pesticides can 
be used to kill them or keep them away from the plants. 
Mining is extracting valuable materials from 
the earth. Drills and explosives are used to 
dig down and create the mines 
underground.  
Mining seeks to find both precious stones 
like diamonds, sapphires, and rubies as well 
as ore – a type of rock that contains 
minerals including metals like iron or 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
copper. The ore must then be processed to remove and purify the useful 
metal. 
Stone that is used for construction and building materials is usually taken not 
from a mine, but instead from the surface of the earth, from a quarry.

Lesson 18: Newspaper English 
If you’ve ever read the news in English, you may have noticed that there are 
some changes in the vocabulary and grammar of newspaper English – 
especially in the headlines, the titles of the articles.  
Because space is at a premium, articles, prepositions, and auxiliary verbs are 
often omitted from headlines: 
• Man Killed in Accident 
A man was killed in an accident 
• Expert Claims Cell Phones Dangerous 
An expert claims that cell phones are dangerous 
• President Caught in Scandal 
The President was caught in a scandal 
To add action and urgency, verbs are often in the present, even when the 
event was in the past: 
• Local Woman Wins $10M in Lottery 
A local woman has won $10M in the lottery 
• President Visits Asia 
The president visited Asia recently 
For events in the future, headlines often use to + base form of the verb 
instead of “will” or “going to”: 
• President to Visit Asia 
The president will visit Asia in the future 
• Apple to Reveal New iPhone on Friday 
Apple will reveal the new iPhone on Friday 
Finally, headlines use strong, simple words rather than longer or vaguer 
expressions. For example: 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• Police Probe Corruption Claims 
The police are investigating corruption claims

Lesson 19: Other Ways to Say… 
This lesson will introduce you to a number of new alternatives for “simple” 
words in English. Many of them have slight differences in the ways in which 
they are used. 
Looking 
If you glance at someone/something, it means you look 
at it quickly for a short time. For example, “I didn’t have 
time to read the newspaper today – I just glanced at the 
headlines.” 
The word glimpse is similar – to look at something/someone quickly for a 
short time, but usually implies that you got an incomplete view of the 
person/object. It’s also used in the expression “catch a glimpse.” For example, 
“There are a number of trees right outside my window, but sometimes I can 
catch a glimpse of the ocean.” 
To peek or peep means to look at something secretly. You might catch your 
kids “peeping” at you when you’re trying to wrap their Christmas presents – 
they are curious about the presents, but they don’t want you to notice that 
they are watching. 
If you look at something for a long time, with steady intention and without 
looking away, you are staring at it. “I can’t stand people who stare at their cell 
phones while talking to me.” 
To look at someone or something intensely and with anger is to glare – for 
example, you might glare at your best friend if they make an annoying 
comment about you in front of other people. 
To look at something with surprise/amazement (or mindlessly) – often with 
your mouth open – is to gape or gawk. When there is an accident, passers-by 
frequently stop and “gawk” at the situation. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
Finally, we have the words gaze and contemplate, meaning to look at 
something thoughtfully or peacefully for a long time. You might gaze at a 
beautiful sunset, for example. 
Walking / Running 
Why walk when there are so many more interesting words to use 
for this action? You can stroll, saunter, or mosey – that means to 
walk in a casual, relaxed way. On a summer afternoon, you might 
“stroll” through the park, without needing to hurry. 
Walking faster and with more intention is called striding or 
marching – if you’re not happy with the customer service in a 
store, you might stride to the manager’s office to make a 
complaint. The word “march” also refers to members of the military walking 
in unison. 
If you’re drunk, very tired, or otherwise unstable, you would stagger or totter 
– that means to walk while almost losing your balance and falling. 
If you were trying to walk very quietly, you would creep or tiptoe – these 
words mean to walk silently and carefully, so as not to disturb someone. “I 
tiptoed out of the room so as not to wake up the baby.” 
Someone who is walking arrogantly, aiming to show off and impress other 
people, is strutting or parading. Maybe your co-worker was recently 
promoted, and now he’s strutting around the office giving everyone else 
orders. 
 
Peacocks are said to "strut" to show off their feathers! 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
For running – usually running very fast – we can use the verbs sprint, dash, 
race, or bolt. “I sprinted to the station to catch the last train before it left.” 
 
Talking 
We have different words for the volume of speech as well 
as its content. 
To yell, scream, shout, or shriek is to speak very loudly, 
for example, “The captain of the soccer team shouted 
instructions to the other players.” Shriek is usually high-
pitched, often by a woman. 
To murmur, mutter, and mumble mean to speak in a 
quiet voice, without opening your mouth much. You usually do this when you 
don’t necessarily want other people to overhear you. “Murmur” is more 
neutral, “mutter” usually means you are saying something negative, and 
“mumble” usually means you are ashamed or you have low self-confidence. 
And to whisper is to speak extremely quietly – you should whisper to another 
person while watching a movie, so that you don’t disturb the other people in 
the audience. 
Now let’s look at the content of what’s being said. Instead of always saying “He 
said” or “She said,” you can use these more descriptive words: 
• boast / brag – To talk arrogantly about something. “James is constantly 
bragging about all the athletic awards he won in college.” 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• whine / grumble – To complain, to comment on the negative aspects of 
something. “Sheila’s always whining about how awful her husband is. I 
don’t know why she doesn’t just leave him, if she’s so unhappy.” 
• pledge / swear / vow – To promise to do something (the last two 
words are the strongest). “He swore to get revenge on his business 
partner, who had stolen from the company.” 
• mention / comment – To say something briefly, without talking about 
it for a long time. “She mentioned that she would be traveling next 
month.” 
• beg / implore – To ask someone insistently with a lot of emotion. “My 
best friend begged me not to tell anyone her secret.” 
• chatting / gabbing – These words describe an informal conversation: 
“On Sunday nights, I like to hang out with my neighbors, chatting about 
the latest TV shows.” 
Laughing and Crying 
To suddenly start laughing very hard is to crack up – 
“The whole class cracked up when the teacher spilled 
her coffee all over her desk.” To laugh mildly (not 
intensely) is often described as chuckling, and to laugh 
with short, high-pitched sounds is called giggling (this 
word is often used for girls’ laughter). 
If you laugh and try to hide it – this is called snickering – especially if you are 
laughing about someone else. “I snickered when I noticed that the boss had a 
big piece of spinach stuck in his teeth.” 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
A person who is laughing very hard and very loudly is howling or roaring 
with laughter – and someone who can’t stop laughing can be described as 
being “in stitches” – especially the kind of laughter where your sides begin to 
hurt. 
On the opposite end of the spectrum, a person who is 
crying very hard can be said to be sobbing or weeping. 
“Sobbing” usually means you are making sounds of 
distress or pain, whereas “weeping” is a quieter 
expression of sadness. Bawling, howling, and wailing 
can also be used for very LOUD crying, without restraint. These words are 
often used when a baby is crying very loudly. 
When you become so overwhelmed with emotion that you have difficulty 
speaking, and you might start crying, this is called getting “choked up.” If a 
person suddenly starts crying, we say they “burst into tears.”  
Eating / Drinking 
If a person eats fast and greedily, we say they 
devour, gobble down, or wolf down their food. 
A slang word used for this type of eating is 
“inhale” – for example, “My son inhaled his 
dinner and ran out the door to meet his friends” – 
it implies that the person ate as fast as simply 
taking a breath! 
When you’re eating something especially 
delicious or fancy, you can say you feasted on the 
food. “In Argentina, we feasted on some of the best steak I’ve ever tasted.” 
If a person is eating very little, then they are nibbling or picking at their food. 
The verb “nibble” implies taking very small bites, and the expression “picking 
at” food usually means that the person has no appetite or doesn’t want to eat. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
Finally, eating casually is described as snacking on or munching on the food 
item: you munch on popcorn while watching a movie. 
Drinking something very fast can be described as gulping 
down or guzzling down the beverage. The opposite of 
that is sipping, which means to drink very slowly in small 
portions. You would sip a glass of fine wine, and it might 
take you an hour to finish it.

down, guzzle down, sip

Lesson 20: Connotations 
The English language is exceptionally rich in vocabulary. Although many 
words express the same or a similar concept, they often have different 
connotations.  
Connotations are the cultural or emotional associations that words bring to 
your mind. Connotations can be positive, negative, or neutral – and the 
selection of one word over another can give a particular tone to your text or 
communicate additional meaning “between the lines.”  
For example, if you are describing a person who is confident, direct and not 
afraid to go after what he wants, you can say he is “assertive” (this implies his 
confidence/directness is a good quality, and shows initiative) or that he is 
“pushy” (this implies that his confidence/directness is a bad quality, because 
it is annoying and he wants to control everything). 
Consider the various shades of meaning for synonyms of the word “thin,” 
which is the opposite of “fat.” The word “thin” has a neutral connotation. 
However, you can also describe someone as: 
• skinny – This implies that they are too thin, or underweight. For 
example, your mother might say, “You should eat more – you’re too 
skinny!” 
• scrawny – This implies a lack of muscle. A girl might say about a guy, 
“I’m not really attracted to him – he’s so scrawny. I prefer athletic guys.” 
• wiry / lean – This means thin and muscular; probably someone who 
does a lot of physical activity and is strong but not bulky. 
• slim – Thin with a positive connotation – thin and attractive. 
• slender / svelte – Thin and graceful/beautiful. “Svelte” adds an extra 
touch of being fashionable/sexy. 
• petite – Thin and short 
• lanky – Thin and tall 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• gaunt – Thin and bony, as if the person is sick or undernourished (so 
their bones start to appear) 
• skeletal – So extremely thin that you can see a lot of bones, someone 
who is starving and possibly near death 
Connotations can be hard to master, because they are often determined by 
culture and common use – and they can differ from person to person. 
Sometimes you can understand them from the context. 
Consider these three sentences: 
• That hotel was a real bargain! We stayed for two whole weeks for less 
than $500. 
• I’m looking for an inexpensive hotel in Madrid. Do you have any 
recommendations? 
• We stayed in a cheap hotel next to the highway. It was noisy, the A/C 
was broken, and they ran out of coffee at breakfast. 
“A bargain,” “inexpensive,” and “cheap” all mean essentially the same thing – 
not costing very much money. But you can understand from the context that 
“a bargain” is described as a great thing, “inexpensive” is neutral, and “cheap” 
is used as a criticism of the hotel’s low quality. 
The Power of Words 
Connotations can be extremely politically and emotionally charged. 
Depending on your perspective… 
• The same person could be described as either a “terrorist” (negative) or 
a “freedom fighter” (positive) 
• The same event could be described as a “riot” (negative) or a 
“demonstration” (positive) 
• The same action could be described as “spying” (negative) or as 
“observing/monitoring” (positive) 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
Words are often intentionally chosen to make the reader/listener feel a 
certain way. One article, complaining about the large number of drug addicts 
on the streets, might call these people “druggies” or “junkies.” Another article, 
which wants us to feel more compassion, may call them “substance abusers” 
instead. 
Consider these different words for women: 
• lady – The most courteous and positive way to refer to a woman 
• woman – The normal, neutral word 
• girl – Some women get offended when men refer to mature women as 
“girls,” as if they were young. However, many women refer to their own 
groups of friends as “girls” or “gals.” 
• chick – This is a slang term, and can be positive or negative – “a hot 
chick” or “an ugly chick” – in either case, it is somewhat dehumanizing 
• bitch – Extremely offensive and derogatory word 
Can you see why it’s very important to know the connotations of the words 
you’re using?

Lesson 21: Noun-Verb Vocabulary 
Builder 
There are a number of words in English that are both nouns and verbs, with 
essentially the same meaning. For example: 
• The rebels attacked the government building.  
(attack = verb) 
• Twenty people were killed in the attack.  
(attack = noun) 
As you can see, the verb form of “attack” refers to the action, and the noun 
form of “attack” refers to the event; the incident when that action happened. 
Here are a few more examples of words that are both nouns and verbs with 
related meanings: 
• I’m renting an apartment. The rent is $800 per month. 
• He never answers his e-mails. I’m still waiting for an answer to a 
message I sent three weeks ago. 
• I have so many hopes and dreams. I’m hoping I can reach my goals this 
year. 
• It’s a very long drive, so we should start driving early in the morning. 
However, there are also a number of words in which the meanings of the noun 
form and the verb form are not so directly related. Consider this example: 
• The boxer hit his opponent. 
hit (verb) = punch, make a violent impact 
• The movie Titanic was a hit. 
hit (noun) = a big success, something popular 
Often, one of the forms is more informal – as is the case with “hit” referring to 
something popular or successful. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
In this lesson you’re going to learn 10 verbs that appear to be nouns, and 10 
nouns that appear to be verbs. This lesson takes the form of two quizzes – 
what I call “discovery” quizzes, because you haven’t learned the words yet.  
You’ll see an example sentence, and you have to make your best guess about 
what the word means in that situation. This is important because it helps you 
train your ability to think about and understand words from their context. 
After you’ve given each quiz your best effort, check your answers and read or 
watch the explanation for more information about the words. 
 
Quiz #1 – Nouns that look like verbs

have to be replaced before long.

cut of future profits… I didn’t take the job.

catch =  
a) hidden disadvantage 
b) reason for not doing something 
c) agreement between seller and buyer

b) pause or interval

fly =

c) bacteria

a) a bag containing a product

We need to remove some of the branches of that tree, so we'll

a) safety equipment 
b) a tool used for cutting

Answers & Explanation – Quiz #1 
1. This part of the machinery is showing quite a bit of wear. It’ll probably 
have to be replaced before long. 
wear = b) damage from use 
“Wear” refers to the normal, gradual damage that occurs as you use something 
for a very long time. It can also be called “wear and tear.”  
 
2. The startup wanted me to design their website for free in exchange for a 
cut of future profits… I didn’t take the job. 
cut = a) portion 
The noun form of “cut” has two meanings. In this context, it means a portion of 
money. Another example is when you buy a flight through a travel agency, the 
travel agent receives a “cut” of the profits (such as a 15% commission). 
Another way to use “cut” as a noun is as a reduction. For example, the 
company is making cuts in all the departments’ budgets. 
 
3. At that store, you can buy the washing machine at 70% off the normal 
price, but the catch is that it doesn’t come with a warranty – so if it 
breaks, you need to pay for the repairs yourself. 
catch = a) hidden disadvantage 
A very common phrase spoken when considering an opportunity that seems 
too good to be true is, “What’s the catch?” – for example, if your friend wants 
to sell you a car for only $200, you would ask, “What’s the catch?” because 
you’d be suspicious that there was some hidden problem with the car… or that 
your friend expected you to do some big favor in return. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
 
4. The government is considering new gun control laws in the wake of the 
recent school shooting. 
wake = a) time after; result 
“In the wake of” means “as a result of” or “in the time shortly after” an event or 
situation. If the president of a company is caught doing something wrong, he 
might resign in the wake of the scandal. 
Another common expression with “wake” is when an event leaves some result 
(usually a bad one) “in its wake” (that is, after it passes). For example, a 
tornado leaves destruction in its wake. A war might leave many orphans in 
its wake.  
The noun “wake” is also used for the disturbance of water that follows a boat: 
 
After the boat passes, it leaves this disturbance of water after it, as a result. 
 
5. Although the university as a whole isn’t particularly famous, its theater 
program is a real draw for students interested in launching acting 
careers. 
draw = c) something that attracts people 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
Although you might know the definition of the verb “draw” as creating a 
picture with pen, pencil, marker, etc. there is another meaning – to attract 
people. It can be used as either a noun or a verb with this meaning: 
• The famous band will draw a large crowd to the festival. 
• We should get that band to play at the festival – it will be a big draw. 
 
6. Saturday morning English classes are exhausting – they’re four solid 
hours without a break. 
break = b) pause or interval 
It’s common to say “Let’s take a 10-minute break” when you want to pause an 
activity (like a meeting or class) for a short time. People also talk about taking 
a “coffee break” or “cigarette break” when you pause to have some coffee or 
smoke a cigarette. 
 
7. I know you don’t like your food too spicy, so I only used a couple drops 
of hot pepper sauce. 
drops = c) small units of liquid 
This is pretty self-explanatory:  
 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
It can be used for any liquid (not just water) – a drop of sauce, a drop of blood, 
a drop of paint, etc. The related verb is drip. 
8. Make sure you cover the food at the picnic to keep the flies off it. 
A fly is a specific type of insect: 
 
 
9. After I paid for the shoes, the cashier handed me my change and a 
receipt. 
change = c) excess money returned to the customer  
Let’s say the shoes cost $17, and you pay for them with a $20 bill. You will 
then have the excess money ($3) returned to you. This money that you get 
back because you paid more than necessary is called “change.” 
 
10. 
 We need to remove some of the branches of that tree, so we'll 
have to buy a saw. 
saw = b) a tool used for cutting 
The noun “saw” refers to a type of tool used for cutting 
things – it has a metal blade with sharp “teeth.” There are 
different types of saws; the simple ones are operated by 
hand, and others are powered by electricity or gas.

1. We’ll have to table the discussion about our website redesign; there are 
far more pressing issues that need our attention.

a) prolong 
b) initiate 
c) postpone 
 
2. The investigation of the crime was delayed after it was discovered that 
the evidence had been doctored. 
doctored =  
a) eliminated 
b) falsified or changed 
c) invented to deceive someone 
 
3. Ever since her husband was diagnosed with cancer, Mary has had to 
shoulder all the work and family responsibilities. 
shoulder =  
a) accept help from others 
b) delay 
c) take on 
 
4. I’m trying to picture my father taking a dance class and I just can’t do it 
– he wouldn’t dance if you paid him! 
picture =  
a) convince 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
b) imagine 
c) invite 
 
5. My legs were caked with mud after I rode my bike through the woods. 
caked =  
a) wet 
b) covered  
c) protected 
 
6. I don’t like the way that lawyers try to milk their clients for every last 
dollar. 
milk =  
a) get as much as possible out of a situation 
b) treat a person in an unprofessional way 
c) charge outrageously expensive prices 
 
7. We store extra office supplies in the basement – feel free to grab paper, 
pens, or whatnot if you run out. 
store =  
a) sell 
b) throw away 
c) keep in reserve 
 
8. After work, I’m heading to the gym. I should be home around 8. 
heading =  
a) going  


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
b) exercising 
c) stopping quickly at a place

speculation that he might be gay.

a) confirming 
b) creating 
c) stimulating, encouraging

 The school is adopting stricter rules in an effort to curb cheating 
on exams.

a) restrain, prevent from increasing 
b) make something impossible 
c) punish wrongdoing 
 
Answers & Explanation – Quiz #2 
1. We’ll have to table the discussion about our website redesign; there are 
far more pressing issues that need our attention. 
table = c) postpone 
“Table” as a verb is typically used in the context of postponing a discussion 
item during a meeting, or postponing consideration of a proposed law. 
 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
2. The investigation of the crime was delayed after it was discovered that 
the evidence had been doctored. 
doctored = b) falsified or changed 
When some official information – such as evidence in a criminal investigation, 
sales figures, results of scientific research, etc. – is purposefully altered in 
order to influence the results, we say the information has been “doctored.” 
 
3. Ever since her husband was diagnosed with cancer, Mary has had to 
shoulder all the work and family responsibilities. 
shoulder = c) take on 
We usually talk about “shouldering” either responsibilities or blame. It means 
to take on or to “carry” the responsibilities or blame – like you would carry a 
heavy burden on your shoulder. 
 
4. I’m trying to picture my father taking a dance class and I just can’t do it 
– he wouldn’t dance if you paid him! 
picture = b) imagine 
To “picture” as a verb means to imagine, to create a mental picture of some 
situation. 
 
5. My legs were caked with mud after I rode my bike through the woods. 
caked = b) covered 
To be “caked” in a substance means to be covered in thick layers of it.  
 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
6. I don’t like the way that lawyers try to milk their clients for every last 
dollar. 
milk = a) get as much as possible out of a situation 
“Milk” as a verb is used for the action of getting milk out of a cow: 
 
When you milk a cow, you keep going until there is no more milk to be 
extracted.  
In the same way, if you “milk” a situation, it means you try to take as much 
advantage of it as possible. It is not necessarily always related to money. For 
example, a person who becomes unexpectedly famous from an internet video 
can try to “milk” their fame (use it to maximum capacity) in order to get 
additional opportunities or stay in the spotlight. 
 
7. We store extra office supplies in the basement – feel free to grab paper, 
pens, or whatnot if you run out. 
store = c) keep in reserve 
The verb “store” means to put objects that you are not currently using in a 
place where you can access them later, when they are needed. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
 
8. After work, I’m heading to the gym. I should be home around 8. 
heading = a) going 
“Head” as a verb is an informal way to say “go” and is used with “to + 
destination,” as in the example – “I’m heading to the gym.” If you’re leaving a 
place, you can say “I’m heading out.” 
 
9. The actor’s sudden divorce from his supermodel wife is fueling 
speculation that he might be gay. 
fueling = c) stimulating, encouraging 
Just like fuel (n.) provides power for a vehicle or machine, the verb “fuel” is 
used when something stimulates or encourages speculation, debate, rumors, 
demand, opposition, etc. 
 
10. 
The school is adopting stricter rules in an effort to curb cheating 
on exams. 
curb = a) restrain; prevent from increasing 
The noun form of “curb” refers to this barrier on the side of a street: 
 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
In a similar way, “curb” as a verb means to implement some sort of barrier to 
restrain or reduce some activity, or prevent the activity from increasing out of 
control. For example, if you are saving up to take a big vacation, then you need 
to curb your spending in daily life.

Lesson 22: Word Roots 
A “root” is the basic linguistic unit of a word, after the prefixes and suffixes are 
removed. Consider the word unhappiness. 
un  
+  
happy     +  ness 
(prefix) 
   (root) 
(suffix) 
Today’s lesson will focus on roots, and the next two lessons will discuss 
common prefixes and suffixes. 
A root may be an entire word, as in the example of happy / unhappiness. 
However, it can also be a word part – as in the example of vis, which means 
“see”: 
• Vision = your ability to see 
• Visual = relating to the sense of sight 
• Invisible = something that cannot be seen 
Many of the word roots in English come from Latin and Greek. Knowing the 
most common roots can give you a clue as to the meaning of new words when 
you come across them. 
Here’s an example. Based on these three words, what do you think the root 
phon means? 
• telephone 
• microphone 
• phonetic 
The root phon means “sound” – a telephone transmits sound, a microphone 
amplifies sound, and “phonetic” refers to the sounds of speech. So when you 
see the word cacophony, you can recognize the root phon and know that it 
has something to do with sound – and maybe guess the rest from the context.  


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
A cacophony is a sound that is harsh and discordant (not pleasant or 
melodious); for example, if there’s a big traffic jam and all the cars are honking 
their horns repeatedly, that’s a cacophony. 
In today’s lesson I’m going to teach you fourteen word roots in English by 
showing you three common words and asking you to guess what the root 
means. Then I’ll reveal the answer and teach you a new word that includes 
this root. 
1. ARCH = _____________________ 
• monarch  
• hierarchy  
• archenemy  
2. BENE = _____________________ 
• benefit  
• benevolent  
• benediction  
3. CHRON = _____________________ 
• chronological  
• chronicle  
• synchronize  
4. CRED = _____________________ 
• incredible  
• discredit  
• credibility  
5. DICT = _____________________ 
• contradict  
• dictate  
• predict   


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
6. JUR/JUS = _____________________ 
• jury  
• justice  
• unjust  
7. LOG = _____________________ 
• logic  
• psychology  
• analogy  
8. LUM/LUC = _____________________ 
• illuminate  
• luminous  
• translucent  
9. MAL = _____________________ 
• malnourished  
• malfunction  
• malevolent  
10. PATH = _____________________ 
• sympathize  
• pathetic  
• empathy 
11. PORT = _____________________ 
• transportation  
• export  
• airport 
12. SCRIB/SCRIP = _____________________ 
• manuscript  


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• inscribe  
• scripture  
13. VAC = _____________________ 
• vacuum 
• evacuate  
• vacancy  
14. VOC/VOK = _____________________ 
• vocalize 
• advocate  
• provoke  
 
ANSWERS 
ARCH = RULER 
• monarch = king or queen 
• hierarchy = order of power 
• archenemy = primary enemy 
The word anarchy refers to an absence of rule or of control, especially a 
political philosophy with no rulers or governments. 
BENE = GOOD 
• benefit = a good result 
• benevolent = showing goodwill 
• benediction = a blessing 
The word benefactor means someone who gives aid – especially financial aid. 
Ex) The donation was made by an anonymous benefactor. 
CHRON = TIME 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• chronological = in the order of time 
• chronicle = a record of a time period 
• synchronize = put into the same time/rhythm 
An anachronism is something that seems to exist outside its proper time. Ex) 
In a world of tablet computers and tiny MP3 players, a cassette tape is an 
anachronism. 
CRED = BELIEF 
• incredible = amazing, difficult to believe 
• discredit = show to be false, make people not believe in it 
• credibility = ability to be believed/trusted 
The word credentials means evidence or qualifications that show your 
authority or show your ability to be trusted – that people can believe in you. 
Ex) He was hired because he had excellent credentials for the position. 
DICT = SAY/SPEAK 
• contradict = say something opposite 
• dictate = say or read aloud, or give orders 
• predict = say what will happen in the future 
The final statement of judgment in a legal case is called the verdict. This word 
can be used for any final conclusion or opinion, not only in official legal 
situations. 
JUR/JUS = LAW 
• jury = the group of people who hear the evidence and make decisions 
about a case in a court of law 
• justice = related to fairness and conformity to the law 
• unjust = not fair according to the rules/laws 
When someone lies or presents false evidence in court, that is called perjury – 
it’s a crime. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
LOG = STUDY/THOUGHT 
• logic = organized and rational thought/reasoning 
• psychology = the study of the mind 
• analogy = similarity between two concepts 
This is why so many branches of study end in –ology (biology, geology, 
technology)! Here’s a new word with LOG – logistics, meaning the details, 
thought, planning, and organization of the aspects of a complex operation. 
LUM/LUC = LIGHT 
• illuminate = make something light/bright 
• luminous = bright, gives light 
• translucent = a substance that light passes through 
The word lucid can mean clear and easily understood. It is also used for 
somebody who is mentally OK and rational. 
MAL = BAD 
• malnourished = receiving bad nutrition 
• malfunction = not function correctly 
• malevolent = with bad intention 
The word malign means to make bad/evil statements about something. For 
example, a political candidate who can’t refute his opponent’s ideas in logical 
debate may resort to maligning his opponent in the media. 
PATH = FEELING 
• sympathize = feel compassion 
• pathetic = provoking the feeling of pity or scorn 
• empathy = identification with another’s feelings and motives 
Apathy is a condition of having no strong feelings and not caring much. 
People can become apathetic when depressed, when unmotivated, or when 
they simply don’t have much energy. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
PORT = CARRY 
• transportation = something that carries you to another place 
• export = carry something out of a country 
• airport = a place where things are carried by air 
If something is portable, that means it can be carried with you. A piano is not 
portable, but a flute is. 
SCRIB/SCRIP = WRITE 
• manuscript = a written book or document 
• inscribe = to mark or engrave words on/in a surface 
• scripture = writings considered holy/religious 
When you write fast and often sloppily (not neatly or clearly, making it 
difficult to read) then you are scribbling. 
VAC = EMPTY 
• vacuum = pulls things by sucking air into an empty space 
• evacuate = get out of an area 
• vacancy = an open/empty place in a hotel 
If someone makes a vacuous comment or has a vacuous expression on their 
face, it means one that is empty of feeling or meaning. 
VOC/VOK = VOICE 
• vocalize = say something with your voice 
• advocate = use your voice to support or promote a cause/idea 
• provoke = bring about action/feeling (“call forth”) 
The word revoke means to “call back,” to remove or cancel something. If you 
drive drunk, your driver’s license will be revoked. 
 
 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net

Lesson 23: Prefixes 
As you learned in the last lesson, a prefix is placed at the beginning of a word 
to modify its meaning: 
• polite / impolite (not polite) 
• market / supermarket (big market) 
• sleep / oversleep (sleep too much) 
• cultural / multicultural (many cultures) 
• view / preview (view before) 
It’s important to have some notion of these prefixes, since they can make a 
difference between similar-looking words: 
• uninformed = have no information 
• misinformed = have the wrong information 
In today’s lesson, I’m going to teach you twelve prefixes, once again using a 
few words you probably already know, and then adding some new ones.  
1. contra-/counter- = against 
• contradiction = two things that conflict with / go against each other 
• counterattack = return attack against the enemy 
• countercultural = against the dominant culture 
• contraband = items prohibited by law from being imported/exported 
• counterfeit = fake, not real (ex. counterfeit money) 
2. dis- = negation  
• disadvantage = opposite of advantage 
• disapprove = not approve 
• disoriented = not oriented; lost one’s sense of direction 
• do (someone) a disservice = do something that causes harm instead of 
helping 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• disconcerting = makes you uneasy, unsettled emotionally, a bit 
uncomfortable 
3. en-/em- bring into the condition of 
• enrage = make angry 
• envision = imagine 
• entrap = make someone trapped, imprisoned 
• enlighten = give spiritual or intellectual insight/knowledge 
• engrossed = completely occupied or absorbed; it is taking all your 
attention; you’re not easily distracted 
• embitter: cause to become bitter 
• embellish: cause to become beautiful; decorate by adding things 
• embark: enter a ship, set out on a journey 
4. hyper- = more than normal 
hypo- = less than normal 
• a hyperactive child has more energy than normal and has difficulty 
sitting still or being quiet 
• hypertension is the more formal name for high blood pressure 
• to hyperventilate means to be breathing much faster and harder than 
normal (often after exercise that was too intense, or due to emotional 
agitation) 
• hypothermia = abnormally low body temperature. People stranded in 
cold climates often get hypothermia as they wait to be rescued 
• hypocrite = a false person who says one thing and does another; is not 
what he/she pretends to be. Ex) Someone who preaches humility, but 
they themselves are very arrogant. 
• hypochondriac = a person who believes themselves to be sick or likely 
to become sick, even though they have few, minor, or no symptoms  
5. in-/im-/il- = not, without 
• inappropriate = not appropriate 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• imprecise = not precise 
• illiterate = can’t read 
• impasse = a situation where no progress can be made (ex. in 
negotiations) 
in/im/il can also have the meaning like “en”: to bring about: 
• inject = put something in 
• impregnate = to get someone pregnant 
• impoverished = poor, in poverty 
• illuminate = make light, make luminous 
6. inter- = between/among 
intra- = inside/within 
• interactive = action/relation between people/things 
• international = among various countries 
• interdisciplinary = a study involving various disciplines (subjects) 
• intranet = network within a company/organization 
• intravenous = within the vein – usually called IV 
7. out- = surpassing, exceeding 
• outrun = run faster than someone/something else 
• outperform = perform better than someone/something else 
• outweigh = be more important than something else 
There are a few situations where “out” means “outer” or “outside”: 
• outskirts of the city = the outer/most distant parts from the center 
• outpatient = not requiring an overnight hospital stay 
8. pro- = in support of, put forward 
• pro-immigration = in support of immigration 
(When used for "in support of," it often appears with a hyphen.  
The opposite is anti-) 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• prognosis = prediction of a future situation/outcome 
• procrastinate = put tasks forward, in the future 
• proselytize = try to convince someone to join your religion/belief 
9. sub- = lower 
• submarine = vessel that travels under the water 
• substandard = below the standards; not good quality 
• subconscious = below the level of your consciousness/awareness 
• subcontract = contract someone else to do some of the tasks of your 
contract (ex. a company contracts you to design a website, and you 
contract a developer to do part of the programming)  
10. syn-/sym- = together 
• synonyms = two words that mean the same thing 
• symmetrical = a design that is equal/balanced on both sides 
• symphony = a piece of music for an orchestra (instruments playing 
together) 
• symposium = a conference for discussion of a topic 
• synergy = energy from interaction together

• transvestite = someone who dresses in clothing of the opposite gender 
• transgender = someone who identifies as a member of the opposite

• transfusion = transfer of blood from one person to another 
• transplant = to move something from one place to another 
12. fore- = before

• forerunner = something that came before (records were the 
forerunners of CDs)

• foresight = perception of things before they occur

Lesson 24: Suffixes – Part 1 
Suffixes are added to the ends of words, usually to change their grammatical 
function or part of speech. Here’s an example of how one word can take many 
different forms depending on the suffix: 
• Tolerate = verb 
• Tolerance = noun 
• Tolerable = adjective meaning able to be tolerated 
• Tolerant = adjective describing a person who has this quality 
• Tolerantly = adverb meaning “in a tolerant way” 
Today’s lesson will teach you some more advanced suffixes for adjectives, 
adverbs, and verbs – we’ll leave the noun suffixes for tomorrow’s lesson. 
 
Adjective Suffixes 
The suffixes -able/-ible mean “is” or “can be.” This is easy to remember, 
because they’re similar to the word “able”! 
• washable = can be washed 
• preferable = is preferred 
• indispensable = essential (cannot be dispensed with) 
• bio-degradable = can be broken down by natural causes 
• convertible = can be converted 
• irrepressible = cannot be repressed 
• susceptible = easily affected, vulnerable 
• invincible = cannot be defeated/conquered 
The suffix –y is often added to nouns to describe something that has the same 
qualities: 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• You already know that you can describe weather as sunny, windy, 
rainy, or foggy 
• This ending is often used with the tastes and textures of foods. 
Something that is milky is like milk in its color, taste, or texture. Foods 
can also be fruity, nutty, sugary, oily, salty, or fatty. 
• If someone is bossy, it means they are controlling in an annoying way – 
like they are trying to be your boss. 
• Something that is tricky is difficult and/or deceptive. 
Another suffix used to make comparisons is –like. 
• During this course, you’ve already learned the words lifelike (a lifelike 
painting) and childlike (someone with the attitude/temperament of a 
child). 
• The –like suffix is often used when you don’t know exactly what 
something is. Since you can’t name or describe it specifically, you make a 
comparison:  
o This thing is made of a rubber-like substance. 
o I saw a shark-like fish in the water. 
(You can add –like to virtually any noun, usually with a hyphen). 
The suffix –ful means “full of” and the suffix –less means “without”: 
• Someone who is careful has lots of care, and someone who is careless 
has no care. 
• If something is meaningful, it is full of meaning and emotionally 
significant; the opposite is meaningless. 
Some adjectives have only one form (either –ful or –less): 
• A person, comment, or expression that is scornful is full of scorn 
(contempt for something considered bad or inferior) – but there is no 
such word as “scornless.” 
• Someone or something that is nameless has no name, or its name is 
unknown or cannot be mentioned – but there is no such word as 
“nameful.” 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
The suffix –ish is also used to say something has that quality (often just a little 
bit): 
• reddish: somewhat red 
• greenish-yellow: yellow with a little bit of green 
• boyish/girlish: a little bit like a boy/girl 
• sheepish: embarrassed, meek, stupid 
A number of adjectives end in -ic / -ical, such as strategic (has strategy), 
emphatic (with emphasis) and biological (involving biology). 
When the noun already ends in –ic, the adjective becomes –ical: 
• magic/magical 
• critic/critical 
• logic/logical 
• music/musical 
• skeptic/skeptical 
A few words have differences between the –ic form and the –ical form: 
• historical = anything that happened in history 
• historic = something important in history 
• economic = related to the economy 
• economical = money-saving 
The suffix –most is used for direction – namely, the farthest point in a certain 
direction: 
• innermost/outermost 
• topmost/uppermost/bottommost 
• leftmost/rightmost 
• northernmost/southernmost/easternmost/westernmost 
(Ex. Alaska is the northernmost state in the United States) 
Finally, there are a few adjectives that end in –some, which means “inclined 
to” or “causing”: 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• Something that is tiresome makes you tired. 
• Something that is worrisome makes you worried. 
• Someone who is winsome is charming, wins you over and makes you 
like them easily. 
• Someone who is meddlesome tends to meddle – to interfere, usually in 
things that are none of their business. 
 
Adverb Suffixes 
You probably already know that most English adverbs end in -ly (quickly, 
directly, beautifully) – but if the adjective already ends in –y, then the adverb 
form ends in –ily: 
• easy / easily 
• voluntary / voluntarily 
• hasty / hastily 
(quickly, in a rush) 
The suffix –ward means “in that direction”: 
• upward/downward 
• inward/outward 
• forward/backward 
• northward/southward/eastward/westward 
Some people add an –s (upwards, downwards, etc.) – this is acceptable 
informally, but the most typical form is without the –s. 
 
Verb Suffixes 
The most common verb suffix is -ate:  
• imitate: try to act/look exactly like someone/something 
• vaccinate: give a vaccine (against a disease) 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• stagnate: become stagnant (no change, progress, improvement) 
• obliterate: completely destroy 
For verbs ending in –ate, the noun form ends in –ation: imitation, vaccination, 
stagnation, obliteration. Note the change in the word stress:  
• IM – i – tate (v.) 
• i – mi – TA – tion (n.) 
• ob – LIT – er – ate (v.) 
• ob – lit – er – A – tion (n.) 
The second most common verb suffix is -ize:  
• categorize: put into categories 
• destabilize: make unstable (the prefix “de” means “not”) 
• familiarize: make familiar 
• traumatize: cause emotional trauma 
For verbs ending in –ize, the noun form ends in –ization: categorization, 
destabilization, etc. Again we have a change in the word stress: 
• de – STA – bil - ize 
• de – sta – bil – i – ZA - tion 
A slightly less common verb ending is -fy:  
• identify, specify, beautify 
• fortify: make strong 
• stupefy: confuse, astound 
• mollify: to calm in temper/feeling, soothe 
• demystify: make less mysterious 
For verbs ending in –fy, the noun form ends in –fication: identification, 
specification, demystification – and the word stress also changes: 
• FORT – i – fy 
• fort - i – fi – CA - tion 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
Finally, we have a few verbs that end in -en: 
• Changes in color: brighten/darken/whiten/blacken 
• Changes in texture or shape: 
harden/soften/thicken/flatten/straighten 
• A few changes in feeling: gladden/sadden/sicken

Lesson 25: Suffixes – Part 2 
In this lesson, you’ll learn some patterns among the great number of noun 
suffixes in English. 
Noun Suffixes for People 
Some suffixes referring specifically to people are –ician, -ist, -ee, and  
–ant/-ent. 
-ician refers to “one who practices” a certain activity, usually a profession: 
• musician, technician, politician 
• beautician – someone skilled in giving beauty/cosmetic treatments 
• pediatrician – a doctor specializing in treating children 
The -ist suffix is much more common and can be used for professions, beliefs, 
and activities: 
Professions with –ist: 
• artist, dentist, geologist 
• ophthalmologist/optometrist – doctors specializing in eyes, vision, 
and glasses and contact lenses 
• therapist / physical therapist – professional specializing in treatment 
of emotional or physical problems, helping you get back to normal 
-ist for people with certain beliefs: 
• racist, feminist, pacifist 
• nihilist – extreme skeptic that denies all existence and knowledge 
• activist – someone who acts in support of a certain cause/idea 
-ist for people who do certain activities: 
• guitarist, soloist 
• rapist – performs forced sexual relations on another person 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• An Olympic medalist has won a medal in the competition 
-ant/-ent: someone who… 
• servant, merchant, student 
• A contestant on a game show or in a contest is competing to win 
• A dissident is someone who disagrees, especially with the government 
Finally, we have –ee, which often refers to the person who is the object of an 
action:  
• The employer provides the job, the employee is employed 
• The interviewer asks the questions, the interviewee answers them 
• The police detain a person, who is called the detainee 
• Someone who has had a limb amputated is an amputee 
Medical Suffixes 
Three noun suffixes often used in medicine are –ectomy, –itis, and –phobia. 
 -ectomy refers to the surgical removal of a body part, and the most common 
ones are: 
• hysterectomy: removal of the uterus 
• mastectomy: removal of the breasts 
• appendectomy: removal of the appendix, which is attached to your 
intestine 
• vasectomy: removal of part of the male reproductive system, making 
him unable to have any more children 
-itis refers to inflammation. The words most commonly used in daily life are: 
• arthritis: inflammation of the joints, a typical ailment of elderly people 
• bronchitis: serious respiratory infection 
• gingivitis: inflammation of the gums 
• laryngitis: the medical word for “a sore throat” 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• tendonitis: inflammation of a tendon, often caused by repetitive 
motions 
-phobia is more psychological – it means “fear of.” There are hundreds of 
technical terms for various phobias, but some of the most common are: 
• claustrophobia: fear of closed/small spaces 
• homophobia: fear and dislike of homosexuals 
• xenophobia: fear and dislike of strangers/foreigners 
The adjective forms end with –phobic (claustrophobic, homophobic, 
xenophobic). 
Forming Nouns from Other Parts of Speech 
The English language has a few patterns when transforming one part of 
speech into another. 
When forming nouns from adjectives, we often use the suffixes –ness and –
ity:

Lesson 26: Perceptions of the Senses 
Today you'll learn a great variety of words for describing the perceptions of 
the five senses – sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. 
Sight 
If something is easy to see, it can be described as clear or distinct – the 
opposite of distinct is something that is blurry/blurred.  
 
A blurry photo 
A place where there is very little light is dim, and an area that is protected 
from light can be described as shadowy. 
 
 
A dim room and a shadowy area 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
When colors are very strong, we call them bold or vivid colors. The opposite 
is pale or pastel colors, which are very light. Something that is colorless and 
rather ugly can be described as drab (usually brown or grey).  
 
 
 
 
 
bold colors  
 
pastel colors 
 
drab colors 
When something has very small dots of a different color, it is speckled – and 
when the colors are all mixed together and not distinct, it is mottled. 
 
 
 
 
speckled 
 
 
 
 
 
mottled 
When something is a different color from what it is supposed to be (because it 
is dirty or damaged) it is discolored. Your teeth can become discolored from 
coffee, or your ceiling can become discolored due to water damage. 
There are a number of words for light – something that emits a steady light is 
glowing, and something that emits an unsteady light (like a candle) is 
flickering.  


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
 
 
The city lights are glowing; the candle is flickering 
When an object – such as a crystal – reflects light in a pleasant way, it is 
sparkling or glittering. 
 
Touch 
Something that feels slightly wet to the touch is damp or moist. “Damp” has a 
slightly negative connotation, and “moist” is a little more positive. If your 
clothes are damp, they haven’t yet dried completely. But a moist cake is a 
good thing. 
The word gummy describes something that is sticky and soft, like chewing 
gum. A sticky and thick liquid is described as gooey (like honey). 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
 
 
Chewing gum is gummy; honey is gooey 
Something that is smooth and pleasant is silky – like the fabric called silk. 
Something that feels like it is covered with an oily substance is slimy – a word 
with a disgusting connotation. Worms and slugs are slimy. 
 
 
silky  
 
 
 
 
slimy 
Finally, we have things that are soft to the touch. Something like cotton candy 
that is light and airy is fluffy, and something like a marshmallow which is a 
little more solid (but still soft and squeezable) is spongy – like a sponge. 
 
 
Cotton candy is fluffy; marshmallows are spongy 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
Smell / Taste 
English has different words for good and bad smells. If something is aromatic 
or fragrant, it smells nice. A noun for a nice smell is a scent. But if something 
is smelly or stinky, it smells bad. Nouns for unpleasant smells include odor 
and stench. 
Something that tastes good is delicious or tasty. If something looks like it 
tastes good, then you can describe it as mouthwatering. A food that is full of 
flavor is said to be rich – but if it has little or no flavor, it is bland or tasteless. 
A food that looks like it tastes bad is unappetizing – and something that tastes 
so bad it can’t be eaten is unpalatable. Sometimes a food has too much of a 
certain flavor, and in this case you can say the taste or smell is overpowering 
– so strong you can’t stand it. 
When food has gone bad, it tastes and smells rancid, rotten, or spoiled. 
There’s a specific word for bread/crackers that have passed their validity – 
these are stale. 
Sound 
There are tons of words for sounds in English, and many of them sound a little 
like what they are describing. 
We have explosive sounds like boom (for an explosion), bang (for a gunshot 
or a door slamming), and pop (for a noise like a champagne bottle opening). 
 
A champagne bottle goes "pop" 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
Noises for impacts include crash (a violent and noisy impact, where things are 
breaking) and thump/thud for a dull, blunt impact, like when you drop a 
heavy bag on the floor. 
 
Breaking glass makes a crashing sound 
Noises with water include a gurgle (the sound of water flowing through a 
space) and a splash – the sound made when an object/person enters the 
water. 
 
"Splash" refers to both the sound and the liquid that flies up 
Bees make a buzzing sound, machines in operation often make a continuous 
humming or whirring sound, some clocks tick, and a metallic sound is called 
a clang. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
 
 
Bees buzz; machines like a fan hum or whirr 
Finally, a few sounds with air include a hiss (like a snake) and a 
swish/swoosh/whoosh, which is the sound of something moving fast 
through the air. 
 
Snakes hiss

Lesson 27: Academic Expressions 
Today you’ll learn a few of the typical phrases that tend to be used in more 
formal writing and presentation. The expressions in this lesson are especially 
useful for an academic context, although they may be used in business as well 
as in writing any type of formal article or report. 
Make sure to check the lesson text for links to an extensive academic phrase 
bank as well as the Academic Word List, a group of the 570 most commonly-
used words in academic publications. 
This lesson centers around ten words that appear frequently in academic 
papers. 
Argument 
In the context of academics, argument refers to a course of logical reasoning, 
not to a verbal conflict. 
• If an author presents a compelling argument, that means one that is 
powerful and convincing. 
• On the other hand, if the argument is weak in its evidence or logic, then 
it is a tenuous argument. 
• Problems with an argument are called flaws in the argument. 
• Presenting evidence to the contrary is countering or refuting the 
argument. The word “refute” is stronger, meaning to disprove the 
argument; show that it is not true. 
Claim 
A claim is a statement of what someone believes to be the truth – it may be 
correct or incorrect. 
• If there is ample support for a claim, it means there is a lot of evidence 
that shows it is true. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• In contrast, an unsubstantiated claim is one with little or no evidence. 
• When you say that someone’s claim is not correct, you are challenging 
the claim. 
Evidence 
• When there is irrefutable/overwhelming evidence to support a claim, 
it means the evidence is so strong that it is practically impossible to 
argue against it. 
• The opposite is scant evidence – very little evidence. 
• Anecdotal evidence is evidence from anecdotes – peoples’ stories and 
experiences. This may conflict with experimental evidence, which is 
more objective and directly observed. 
• If the evidence corroborates a claim, it means it supports and 
strengthens it. 
Grounds 
“Grounds” refer to the basis or foundation of an argument or belief. 
• After presenting your evidence, you can write, “On these grounds, we 
can conclude that…” 
• If you have reasonable grounds for a conclusion, it means there is 
enough evidence to draw the conclusion (even if the evidence is not 
100% perfect and complete). 
• Ground is also used as a verb: you can say someone’s “views are 
grounded on” (based on) a certain belief or assumption. 
Issue 
Issue is a synonym for a particular subject or matter. 
• When an issue is under scrutiny, it means it is being very carefully 
examined. 
• We say an issue is clouded when it is not clear; it is complex and some 
other factors are interfering. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• The expression an underlying issue refers to one that is at the “root” of 
some problem or situation, although it might not be obvious. 
Literature 
When referring to the literature in an academic/scientific context, we are not 
talking about fiction, but instead the previous publications on the topic. 
• A growing body of literature means that more and more articles and 
books are being published on the topic. 
• If the literature abounds with examples, it means there are MANY 
examples in past publications. 
• When there is a consensus in the literature, it means there is a general 
agreement among authors who have previously studied and written 
about the subject. 
Premise 
A premise is one of the basic points in an argument, often an assumption that 
something is true. 
• If you can infer something from the premises, it means that you can 
get to a logical conclusion starting from the basic points. 
• Sometimes arguments are flawed because they are based on faulty 
premises – premises that are false or problematic. 
Research 
• The verb we usually use with “research” is do, but in a more formal 
context we often say conduct research or perform research. 
• Research that is pioneering or ground-breaking makes new progress 
in an area. 
• The findings of the research are its results or conclusions. 
Study 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
In academic/scientific English, “study” is often used as a noun to refer to the 
project. 
• A preliminary study is one that is done early, before the main research 
is performed. 
• A feasibility study is research done to see if something is feasible 
(possible). 
• One common phrase used to introduce the objectives of a piece of 
academic writing is: “The present study aims to…” 
Note that study is countable, but research is not. You can say “a study,” but 
not “a research.” 
View 
The word “view” is used to refer to a perspective or opinion. 
• The prevailing view is the view held by the majority. 
• If people have divergent views, then their views are different; they 
contrast each other. 
• When you expound on a view, it means you explain it in lots of detail.

Lesson 28: Non-Obvious Binomials 
Binomials are expressions with two words joined by a conjunction. Three 
binomials you probably already know are rock and roll, more or less, and 
step by step. 
With some binomials, it’s easy to figure out what they mean. If someone is 
sick and tired of a situation, it means they are frustrated with it. Talking 
about the ups and downs of an experience means the good moments (“ups”) 
and the bad moments (“downs”). 
This lesson will focus on binomials that are not so obvious – which may be 
difficult to understand based on their words alone. I’ve included some 
examples to better illustrate the use of these expressions. 
Binomials with AND 
• If something is growing or developing by leaps and bounds, it is 
progressing very fast. Both “leap” and “bound” refer to a big jump 
forward. 
 
• The expression every nook and cranny of a place means every possible 
tiny space in that location. If you lost your keys, you would look in every 
nook and cranny of your house in order to find them! 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• Pins and needles refers to that tingling sensation felt in your hand or 
foot after it loses circulation. This expression is also used 
metaphorically – if you are on pins and needles, it means you are in a 
state of excited anticipation. 
 
• If a situation is touch and go, it means it is in a delicate or risky state. If 
someone is very sick and in danger of dying, doctors would say their 
condition is “touch and go.” 
• The nuts and bolts of something are its basics – you might have a good 
knowledge of the nuts and bolts of English grammar. This expression 
comes from the fact that nuts and bolts are essential parts of a machine. 
 
• A bait and switch is a deceptive strategy where you present an 
attractive offer, but then when the person becomes interested, you 
change it or try to make them do something else. If a store advertises 
cell phones on sale for $10, but in reality you can only get the $10 cell 
phone if you sign up for a $75/month contract, that’s a bait and switch 
tactic. 
 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
Binomials with OR/NOR 
• The phrase take it or leave it is often said when presenting an offer 
that the other person must either accept or reject; there is no room for 
negotiation. If you’re selling a watch, and the buyer is pressuring you for 
a discount, you could say “The price is $100. Take it or leave it.” 
• Somewhat similar to that is no ifs, ands, or buts, meaning there is no 
room for negotiation after giving a command. Your boss might want a 
project finished by Friday, no ifs, ands, or buts. It means the deadline is 
not extendable and no excuses will be accepted. 
• If you say you will do something come hell or high water, it means you 
are extremely determined and you will do it no matter what – 
regardless of difficulties or challenges. 
• The expression sink or swim is used metaphorically to mean succeed 
or fail based on your own efforts or abilities. Many parents help their 
children with homework, but when their kids go to college, it’ll be “sink 
or swim” – they must succeed or fail in their own merit. 
Binomials with Alliteration 
Alliteration is the repetition of the same sound at the beginnings of words. 
• Tossing and turning is when you can’t sleep, often because of worry – 
you turn from side to side in bed, but you just can’t relax or get 
comfortable. 
• To hem and haw is to speak with lots of hesitations, saying “um” and 
“ah” a lot, often because you are uncomfortable with the topic or trying 
to avoid saying something directly. Your co-worker might hem and haw 
if you point out a mistake in his work and he tries to explain it. 
• If something is without rhyme or reason, it is completely disorganized 
or has no purpose. If you write a report with no rhyme or reason, it has 
no logical order. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• Feast or famine means that sometimes there is too much of something, 
and other times there is too little. If you are a freelancer and you are 
overworked one month, but have no projects the next, you could say 
“It’s feast or famine.” 
• When someone is ranting and raving, they are wildly shouting or 
complaining about something that angers them. Someone with very 
strong political views might rant and rave about people who hold the 
opposite beliefs. 
• Something that is tried and true is dependable, it has been tested and 
proven to be good. For example, if a recipe is tried and true, it means 
that many people have used it successfully to cook a great meal. 
• If something is part and parcel of an experience, it means it’s a 
necessary part of the experience and cannot be avoided. Sleepless nights 
are part and parcel of having a new baby. 
Rhyming Binomials 
• Hustle and bustle refers to confusion and chaos in a busy place. New 
York City has a lot of “hustle and bustle,” but a small town in the 
mountains does not. 
• If you wine and dine someone, it means you entertain them with a 
fancy and expensive meal. Businesses often wine and dine potential 
clients or partners. 
 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• Doom and gloom refers to a depressing feeling that a situation is bad 
and not likely to improve. If you have a pessimistic friend, you would tell 
them to cheer up because life is not all doom and gloom. 
• When someone acts high and mighty, it means they behave as though 
they are superior to others. Some people who go to a prestigious 
university act all high and mighty because they attended a famous 
school. 
• Leaving someone high and dry means to leave them in a difficult 
situation without any help. If you’re traveling in a foreign country, a 
dishonest taxi driver might leave you high and dry in a completely 
unknown part of the city. 
• If you say “it’s my way or the highway,” you are requiring other people 
to do what you want, or else they will have to leave or be excluded.

Lesson 29: Metaphors 
A metaphor is an expression that uses a quality of one thing (usually a more 
physical or concrete thing) to represent a less concrete thing or idea. Put more 
simply - metaphors create a "mental picture" that helps illustrate a concept. 
For example, we can say someone is experiencing a roller coaster of 
emotions. This expression uses a physical object - a roller coaster - to 
illustrate the idea that emotions are going up and down very quickly and 
unpredictably. 
 
A lot of phrasal verbs are used metaphorically. Compare these two sentences: 
• The tanks shot down two of the 
enemy aircraft. 
• My boss shot down every single 
one of my suggestions. 
To shoot down an idea or suggestion 
means to reject or discredit it, destroying it in the same way you would shoot 
down an airplane during a war. 
 
 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
 
Metaphors for People 
• She’s an angel. = She’s very good and kind, or she helped/saved you in a 
bad situation. 
 
• He’s a pig. = He is rude, gross, or greedy. 
 
• She’s a chicken. = She’s a coward, has no courage. 
 
• I’m a night owl. = I like to stay up late; I have lots of energy at night. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
 
• My boss is an ogre. = My boss is cruel, monstrous, and demanding. 
 
• Turned out I was just a pawn in his game. = He used and manipulated 
me to gain some greater advantage for himself. 
 
A “pawn” is this piece in a chess game. 
• He has a heart of gold. = He has a kind and generous character. 
• She has a heart of stone. = She has no emotion, no compassion. 
• He was a late bloomer. = He developed his best skills/abilities later 
than “normal.” 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
 
When a flower “blooms,” it opens 
• You’re on fire! = You’re especially filled with inspiration and energy. 
 
• You’re on a roll! = You’re having a period of one success after another. 
 
 
Metaphors for Situations 
A dry spell is a long period without success – alluding to a lack of rain making 
it difficult to grow crops. Someone who hasn’t been in a romantic relationship 
for the past three years is going through a dry spell. 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
If there’s a tidal wave of something, it means there’s a LOT of it coming in. 
Can be good or bad – a tidal wave of donations for a child with cancer, or a 
tidal wave of violent crime. 
 
The literal meaning of the word minefield is an area where there are 
explosives buried underground – but the word is used metaphorically to mean 
a situation that is full of potential dangers. 
By contrast, something that is smooth sailing is easy with no problems 
during the process, in the same way that a ship sailing through smooth (calm) 
waters will have a tranquil voyage. 
 
When sailing, you do not want your boat to hit any rocks in the water – and in 
the English language the concept of “rocks” is often used for difficulty: 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• A marriage that is on the rocks is 
having major problems. 
• A rocky relationship is full of 
problems, and a rocky start to 
something means it didn’t start very 
successfully. 
• If you are between a rock and a hard place, it means you have 
unpleasant options and no good way to avoid them. If you have a great 
job in a city you love, but your parents want you to move back to your 
hometown, you are between a rock and a hard place because you will 
either have to give up the job or anger your parents. 
In mythology, a silver bullet is the only thing that can kill a vampire or 
werewolf. In English, the expressions silver bullet and magic bullet refer to a 
quick and instant solution to a problem.  
It’s usually used in the negative form to say there’s no easy solution: There’s 
no magic bullet against cancer; the disease has many different forms and 
each one requires specialized treatment. 
We have three very vivid metaphors to describe a process that begins and 
then keeps going: 
• A domino effect / chain reaction is when one event leads to a 
continuing series of other, similar events. Ex) The collapse of the 
country’s government caused a chain reaction of revolutions 
throughout the entire region. 
 


 
 
- EspressoEnglish.net 
• A snowball effect is when something very small begins a process that 
becomes much larger with time – like a snowball getting bigger as it 
rolls down the side of a mountain. Ex) Being bullied as a child can begin 
a snowball effect of mounting insecurity and self-esteem issues that 
can result in professional and relational problems as an adult. 
 
When you are relieved that you don’t have to worry about something or be 
responsible for it any more, you can say it’s a weight off my shoulders. If you 
are very busy at work and your colleague offers to do part of the project 
originally assigned to you, you could say “Thank you so much. That’s a huge 
weight off my shoulders.” 
Finally, most people like listening to music – so when you say a piece of news 
is “music to my ears,” it means it makes you happy to hear it. If you’re hoping 
to go to the beach and someone tells you it’ll be sunny over the weekend, you 
could say “That’s music to my ears!”
